name: Canada
summary: Federally regulated banks are supervised by OSFI for prudential soundness and by FCAC for market conduct under the Bank Act's Financial Consumer Protection Framework (in force June 2022). FINTRAC, the financial intelligence unit, enforces the PCMLTFA, whose Regulations expressly require a written, ongoing compliance training program. Global Affairs Canada administers sanctions, the Privacy Commissioner oversees PIPEDA and the Labour Program enforces the Canada Labour Code. Provincial regulators oversee credit unions, securities and insurance. Explicit training duties sit in the PCMLTF Regulations, Bank Act s. 627.02, PIPEDA and the Labour Code; OSFI guidelines add training expectations for conduct, cyber and resilience.

regulators.name: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
regulators.role: Prudential regulator of federally regulated banks: governance, operational resilience, technology and cyber, third-party risk, integrity and security; receives terrorist and sanctions property reports.

regulators.name: Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada
regulators.role: Financial intelligence unit and AML/ATF supervisor under the PCMLTFA; receives suspicious, large cash and EFT reports and imposes penalties.

regulators.name: Financial Consumer Agency of Canada
regulators.role: Supervises banks' compliance with the Bank Act consumer provisions, including complaints, sales practices, whistleblowing and debt collection.

regulators.name: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
regulators.role: Oversees PIPEDA, including breach reports from private-sector organisations such as banks.

regulators.name: Global Affairs Canada
regulators.role: Administers Canadian sanctions under the Special Economic Measures Act, the Magnitsky Law and the United Nations Act.

regulators.name: Department of Finance Canada
regulators.role: Responsible for AML/ATF policy and the PCMLTFA, including Ministerial directives, and for financial sector legislation such as the Bank Act.

regulators.name: Canada Revenue Agency
regulators.role: Receives FATCA (Part XVIII) and CRS (Part XIX) information returns from financial institutions.

regulators.name: Labour Program, Employment and Social Development Canada
regulators.role: Enforces Part II of the Canada Labour Code, including harassment and violence prevention, for federally regulated employers such as banks.

programs.title: Canada | PCMLTFA Compliance Program and AML Training
programs.why: Every bank must run a PCMLTFA compliance program, and the Regulations expressly require a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees and agents and a documented plan for delivering it. FINTRAC expects the training to cover the Act, the bank's own policies and each person's role in spotting money laundering, at a frequency the bank sets and justifies.

references.provision: Section 156(1)(d) and (e) (training program and plan); 156(3) (two-year review)
references.note: The compliance program must include a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees, agents and others authorised to act for the entity, a documented plan for delivering that training, and a documented effectiveness review at least every two years.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Section 9.6(1) and (1.1) (compliance program); 9.6(3) (special measures for high risk)
references.note: Every reporting entity must establish and implement a compliance program in line with the Regulations; since March 2026 the program must also be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.

references.title: Compliance program requirements
references.note: FINTRAC expects the training program to explain the Act's requirements, the entity's policies on reporting, record keeping and know-your-client, and each person's role in detecting ML/TF; the plan should name recipients (front line, cash handlers, compliance officer, senior management, IT, internal audit), topics, methods and frequency, tailored to ML, TF and sanctions evasion risk.

programs.why: Banks must periodically monitor each business relationship, at a frequency set by their risk assessment, to detect reportable transactions, keep client information up to date, reassess risk and check that activity fits the client profile. Staff who own relationships or review activity need this in their ongoing training.

programs.why: When verifying an entity, banks must obtain the names of directors and of people who own or control 25% or more, take reasonable measures to confirm it, and report material discrepancies with the federal corporate registry. programs.why: Banks must determine whether clients are foreign or domestic PEPs, heads of international organizations, or their family members or close associates, treat foreign PEPs as high risk, and apply senior management approval and source-of-funds steps where required. Staff who open and manage such accounts need targeted training.

programs.title: Canada | Canadian Sanctions Compliance (SEMA, Magnitsky Law, UN Act)
programs.why: Canadian sanctions laws prohibit dealings with listed persons and require banks to keep checking whether they hold listed persons' property and to report it. Since 2024 suspicious transaction reports also cover sanctions evasion, and FINTRAC expects AML training to reflect sanctions evasion risk, but the sanctions statutes themselves do not prescribe training.

notes: PCMLTFA 2024: the Fall Economic Statement Implementation Act, 2023 (assented 20 June 2024) added sanctions evasion to suspicious transaction reporting and let reporting entities share personal information with each other to detect ML, TF or sanctions evasion (s. 11.01); the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 made further changes.

PCMLTFA 2026: the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (assented 26 March 2026) requires compliance programs to be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective, raises maximum penalties (entities: $20 million per violation; cumulative greater of $20 million or 3% of global income) and adds compliance orders; mandatory enrolment of reporting entities with FINTRAC starts on a date to be fixed.

Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (assented 26 March 2026) amended the PCMLTFA (including confidentiality of beneficial ownership discrepancy reports) and the Special Economic Measures Act, and added Bank Act rules on account capabilities and consumer-targeted fraud, including initial and recurrent fraud training; the Bank Act fraud division comes into force on a date to be fixed.
PCMLTF Regulations were amended by SOR/2024-266, SOR/2024-267 (part in force 1 October 2025) and SOR/2025-68; the consolidated Regulations were current to 19 October 2026 when checked.
FCAC published a revised Guideline on Complaint-Handling Procedures in June 2026 with an effective date of 23 June 2027; until then the January 2022 version applies.

OSFI Guideline E-21 (August 2024) was to be fully operational by 1 September 2026; B-13, B-10 and the Integrity and Security Guideline (January 2024) work alongside it. OSFI consulted until 31 October 2026 on a senior leader accountability regime.
CRA guidance on the CRS was revised in July 2026 for Part XIX amendments taking effect on 1 January 2027.
